Everyone I know got handed the most powerful tool of their career with no manual. No training, no onboarding, nothing. One day it just appeared, and everyone started using it their own way.

The industry has systematically failed at modern offline web portability for the last two decades.If you want to distribute a complex, interactive manual or a heavy React dashboard for pure offline use, what are your options?

articles.author: Mike Clarke
articles.description:
Postgres Row-Level Security doesn't raise an error when it blocks you. It returns zero rows. Your query succeeds. Your agent sees an empty queue. Your agent idles. Your jobs pile up.
This is what happened to ARIA, our autonomous AI system at Elevare Digital.
Postgres RLS silently filters rows on SELECT — a blocked read and a genuinely empty table look identical to the caller
An orchestrator that reads its own queue gets no exception, no warning, no non-200 status code when RLS blocks it
A healthy heartbeat on an idle agent tells you nothing about whether the idle is real
The fix: add a canary count that verifies you can read, not just that you did read
Treat an empty read as a question, not an answer
The orchestrator polls a work queue table. Normal operation:
Query for pending jobs
If res…

articles.author: Ameer Abdullah
articles.description:
Tracing a generator's execution reveals a fundamentally different way Python can run code.
A generator function looks like a regular function but behaves in a fundamentally different way. Understanding that difference requires tracing through what Python actually does when it executes one.
A regular function runs to completion when called. A generator function returns an iterator object immediately without running any of its code.
def regular():
    print("regular function running")
    return 42

def generator():
    print("generator running")
    yield 42

r = regular()      # prints "regular function running"
g = generator()    # prints nothing

When you call generator(), Python creates a generator object and returns it. None of the code inside the function has executed yet. The print s…
articles.title: Generator Internals: Why They Are Lazy and What That Actually Means

articles.author: saltmire
articles.description:
Almost every action game needs the same thing: something that deals damage, and
Area2D + CollisionShape2D,
A Hitbox is an Area2D on your attack (a sword swing, a bullet, a stomp).
It only scans — it never needs to be detected.
A Hurtbox is an Area2D on anything that can be damaged. It only needs to
be detected — it never scans.
That split is the trick most tutorials skip, and it's why layers get confusing.
collision_layer is what you are; collision_mask is what you look for. So:
# hurtbox: I exist on layer 20, and I look for nothing.
collision_layer = 0
set_collision_layer_value(20, true)
collision_mask = 0
monitorable = true
monitoring = false

# hitbox: I exist on nothing, and I look for layer 20.
collision_layer = 0
collision_mask = 0
set_collision_mask_value(20, true)
monitoring = true…
